items.readable_text:
Content:
Suppose that [MATH: \mathbf F] is a vector field on [MATH: \mathbb R^2,] expressed in terms of its component functions as

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf F(x,y) = P(x,y)\,\mathbf i + Q(x,y)\,\mathbf j.]

Content:
If the first partial derivatives of [MATH: P] and [MATH: Q] exist, then the divergence of [MATH: \mathbf F,] denoted [MATH: \textrm{div}\,\mathbf F,] is the scalar given by

Content:
[MATH: \textrm{div}\,\mathbf F = \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y}.]

Content:
Notice that if we define the differential operator [MATH: \nabla] (a.k.a. the "del" operator) as

Content:
[MATH: \nabla = \mathbf i\,\dfrac{\partial }{\partial x} + \mathbf j\,\dfrac{\partial }{\partial y},]

Content:
then the divergence of [MATH: \mathbf F] is given by the dot product

Content:
[MATH: \textrm{div}\,\mathbf F = \nabla \cdot \mathbf F.]

Content:
For example, suppose that the vector field [MATH: \mathbf F] is given by

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf F(x,y) = 2xy\, \mathbf i + e^{yx} \, \mathbf j .]

Content:
Then, we can calculate [MATH: \textrm{div}\,\mathbf{F}] using the dot product formula, as follows:

Content:
[MATH: divF|= ∇ ⋅ F; = (i(∂)/(∂x) + j(∂)/(∂y)) ⋅ (2xyi + e^{yx}j); = (∂)/(∂x)(2xy) + (∂)/(∂y)(e^{yx}); = 2y + xe^{yx}]

items.title: Some Important Notes About the Divergence of a Vector Field

sections.normalized_html: There are a few things we should note about the divergence:
sections.readable_text: There are a few things we should note about the divergence:

sections.normalized_html:
• We can only compute the divergence of a vector field, and a vector field's divergence is a scalar field. So if [MATH: G(x,y) = \textrm{div}\,\mathbf F,] then we have the following map: [MATH: \underbrace{\,\,\,\mathbf F(x,y)\,\,\,}_{\textrm{vector field}} \mapsto\underbrace{\,\,\,G(x,y)\,\,\,}_{\textrm{scalar field}}] In contrast, if [MATH: f(x,y)] is a scalar field, then the statement [MATH: \textrm{div}\, f] has no meaning.

  • We can easily extend the notion of divergence to three dimensions. So, if [MATH: \mathbf F(x,y,z) = P\,\mathbf i + Q\,\mathbf j + R\,\mathbf k,] then [MATH: \textrm{div}\,\mathbf F] is given by [MATH: \textrm{div}\,\mathbf F = \nabla\cdot \mathbf F = \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y} + \dfrac{\partial R}{\partial z},] where the three-dimensional differential operator [MATH: \nabla] is given by [MATH: \nabla = \mathbf i\,\dfrac{\partial }{\partial x} + \mathbf j\,\dfrac{\partial }{\partial y} + \mathbf k\,\dfrac{\partial }{\partial z}.]

  • The divergence of a vector field at a point [MATH: P] gives us helpful information about the tendency of the vector field to behave like a source or a sink at [MATH: P.] We'll describe this in more detail shortly.

sections.normalized_html: Consider the vector field [MATH: \mathbf{F}=\ln(2x+y)\,\mathbf{i}+ x^2e^{3y}\,\mathbf{j}.] Evaluate [MATH: \nabla \cdot\mathbf{F}] at the point [MATH: (1,0).]
sections.readable_text:
Consider the vector field [MATH: \mathbf{F}=\ln(2x+y)\,\mathbf{i}+ x^2e^{3y}\,\mathbf{j}.]
Evaluate [MATH: \nabla \cdot\mathbf{F}] at the point [MATH: (1,0).]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
If [MATH: \mathbf{F}=P\,\mathbf{i}+Q\,\mathbf{j}] is a vector field on [MATH: \mathbb{R}^2] and the partial derivatives of the components of [MATH: \mathbf F] all exist, then the divergence of [MATH: \mathbf F] is the scalar field given by

[MATH: \nabla\cdot\mathbf{F}=\textrm{div}\,\mathbf F=\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x}+\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y}.]

Therefore, we have [MATH: ∇ ⋅ F|= (∂P)/(∂x) + (∂Q)/(∂y); = (∂)/(∂x)(\ln (2x + y)) + (∂)/(∂y)(x^{2}e^{3y}); = (2)/(2x + y) + 3x^{2}e^{3y}.]

Finally, we evaluate [MATH: \textrm{div}\,\mathbf {F}] at the point [MATH: (1,0),] and obtain [MATH: (∇ ⋅ F)(1, 0)|= (2)/(2(1) + 0) + 3(1)^{2}e^{3(0)}; = 1 + 3; = 4.]

sections.normalized_html: Consider the vector field [MATH: \mathbf{F}=(2x-y)^2\,\mathbf{i}+(3y-2z)^2\,\mathbf{j}+(x-2z)^2\,\mathbf{k}.] Evaluate [MATH: \textrm{div}\,\mathbf{F}] at the point [MATH: (1,2,1).]
sections.readable_text: Consider the vector field [MATH: \mathbf{F}=(2x-y)^2\,\mathbf{i}+(3y-2z)^2\,\mathbf{j}+(x-2z)^2\,\mathbf{k}.] Evaluate [MATH: \textrm{div}\,\mathbf{F}] at the point [MATH: (1,2,1).]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
If [MATH: \mathbf{F}=P\,\mathbf{i}+Q\,\mathbf{j} + R\,\mathbf k] is a vector field on [MATH: \mathbb{R}^3] and the partial derivatives of the components of [MATH: \mathbf F] all exist, then the divergence of [MATH: \mathbf F] is the scalar field given by

[MATH: \textrm{div}\,\mathbf F = \nabla\cdot\mathbf{F}=\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x}+\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y}+\dfrac{\partial R}{\partial z}.]

Therefore, we have [MATH: ∇ ⋅ F|= (∂P)/(∂x) + (∂Q)/(∂y) + (∂R)/(∂z); = (∂)/(∂x)((2x − y)^{2}) + (∂)/(∂y)((3y − 2z)^{2}) + (∂)/(∂z)((x − 2z)^{2}); = 4(2x − y) + 6(3y − 2z) − 4(x − 2z); = 4x + 14y − 4z.]

Finally, we evaluate [MATH: \textrm{div}\,\mathbf { F}] at the point [MATH: (1,2,1),] and obtain [MATH: divF(1, 2, 1)|= 4(1) + 14(2) − 4(1); = 28.]

Content:
Our goal now is to develop an intuitive understanding of what the divergence of a vector field measures.

Content:
Consider the vector field [MATH: \mathbf F(x,y)] and the point [MATH: S,] shown below. Imagine that this vector field represents the velocity field of a stream of flowing water.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/0ebf9f474e4eac749e182bd3a5ca9607]

Content:
We can see from our diagram that [MATH: S] acts like a source. You can think of this as an open faucet, pushing water onto the plane and away from itself.

Content:
Since [MATH: S] acts like a source, [MATH: \textrm{div}\,\mathbf F] is nonzero. By convention, if a point [MATH: S] acts like a source, the divergence is positive:
[MATH: \textrm{div}\,\mathbf F > 0]
In this particular case, every point in our vector field acts as a source. So [MATH: \textrm{div}\,\mathbf F > 0] everywhere.

Content:
If we reverse the situation, we get the following:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/2318cee55cbaa4a0987c34237058fd13]

Content:
We can see from our diagram that [MATH: T] acts like a sink. You can think of this as an open plughole that sucks in the surrounding water.

Content:
Since [MATH: T] acts like a sink, [MATH: \textrm{div}\,\mathbf F] is also nonzero. By convention, if a point [MATH: T] acts like a sink, the divergence is negative:
[MATH: \textrm{div}\,\mathbf F < 0]
Every point in our vector field acts like a sink in this case. So [MATH: \textrm{div}\,\mathbf F < 0] everywhere.

Content:
Finally, note that if [MATH: \textrm{div}\,\mathbf F = 0] everywhere in the domain of some vector field [MATH: \mathbf F,] we say that [MATH: \mathbf F] is solenoidal.

Consider the vector field [MATH: \mathbf F] shown above. Which of the following statements are true everywhere in the domain of [MATH: \mathbf F?]

1. [MATH: \textrm{div}\,\mathbf F = 0]
2. [MATH: \textrm{div}\,\mathbf F > 0]
3. [MATH: \textrm{div}\,\mathbf F < 0]
4. [MATH: \mathbf F] is solenoidal

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Recall that [MATH: extrm{div}\, \mathbf F = abla\cdot\mathbf F] denotes the divergence of the vector field [MATH: \mathbf F.]

Intuitively, the divergence of [MATH: \mathbf F] at a point [MATH: P] measures how much [MATH: \mathbf F] acts like a source or a sink at [MATH: P\mathbin{:}]

  • If [MATH: \mathbf F] acts like a source at [MATH: P,] then [MATH: abla \cdot \mathbf F > 0] at [MATH: P.]

  • If [MATH: \mathbf F] acts like a sink at [MATH: P,] then [MATH: abla \cdot \mathbf F < 0] at [MATH: P.]

  • If [MATH: \mathbf F] acts like neither a source nor a sink at [MATH: P,] then [MATH: abla \cdot \mathbf F =0] at [MATH: P.]

If [MATH: abla \cdot \mathbf F = 0] everywhere in the domain of [MATH: \mathbf F,] we say that [MATH: \mathbf F] is solenoidal.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement:

  • Statement I is true, whereas statements II and III are false. For any point [MATH: P,] the sum of the inward-pointing vectors equals the sum of the outward-pointing vectors. Therefore, [MATH: \mathbf F] acts neither like a source nor a sink.

  • Statement IV is true. Since [MATH: abla \cdot \mathbf F = 0] everywhere, the vector field [MATH: \mathbf F] is solenoidal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and IV only."

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Suppose that [MATH: \mathbf F] is a vector field on [MATH: \mathbb R^2,] expressed in terms of its component functions as

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf F(x,y) = P(x,y)\,\mathbf i + Q(x,y)\,\mathbf j.]

Content:
If the first partial derivatives of [MATH: P] and [MATH: Q] exist, then the divergence of [MATH: \mathbf F,] denoted [MATH: \textrm{div}\,\mathbf F,] is the scalar given by

Content:
[MATH: \textrm{div}\,\mathbf F = \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y}.]

Content:
Notice that if we define the differential operator [MATH: \nabla] (a.k.a. the "del" operator) as

Content:
[MATH: \nabla = \mathbf i\,\dfrac{\partial }{\partial x} + \mathbf j\,\dfrac{\partial }{\partial y},]

Content:
then the divergence of [MATH: \mathbf F] is given by the dot product

Content:
[MATH: \textrm{div}\,\mathbf F = \nabla \cdot \mathbf F.]

Content:
For example, suppose that the vector field [MATH: \mathbf F] is given by

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf F(x,y) = 2xy\, \mathbf i + e^{yx} \, \mathbf j .]

Content:
Then, we can calculate [MATH: \textrm{div}\,\mathbf{F}] using the dot product formula, as follows:

Content:
[MATH: divF|= ∇ ⋅ F; = (i(∂)/(∂x) + j(∂)/(∂y)) ⋅ (2xyi + e^{yx}j); = (∂)/(∂x)(2xy) + (∂)/(∂y)(e^{yx}); = 2y + xe^{yx}]

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: Some Important Notes About the Divergence of a Vector Field

Content:
There are a few things we should note about the divergence:

Content:
- We can only compute the divergence of a vector field, and a vector field's divergence is a scalar field. So if [MATH: G(x,y) = \textrm{div}\,\mathbf F,] then we have the following map:
[MATH: \underbrace{\,\,\,\mathbf F(x,y)\,\,\,}_{\textrm{vector field}} \mapsto\underbrace{\,\,\,G(x,y)\,\,\,}_{\textrm{scalar field}}]
In contrast, if [MATH: f(x,y)] is a scalar field, then the statement [MATH: \textrm{div}\, f] has no meaning.
- We can easily extend the notion of divergence to three dimensions. So, if [MATH: \mathbf F(x,y,z) = P\,\mathbf i + Q\,\mathbf j + R\,\mathbf k,] then [MATH: \textrm{div}\,\mathbf F] is given by
[MATH: \textrm{div}\,\mathbf F = \nabla\cdot \mathbf F = \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y} + \dfrac{\partial R}{\partial z},]
where the three-dimensional differential operator [MATH: \nabla] is given by
[MATH: \nabla = \mathbf i\,\dfrac{\partial }{\partial x} + \mathbf j\,\dfrac{\partial }{\partial y} + \mathbf k\,\dfrac{\partial }{\partial z}.]
- The divergence of a vector field at a point [MATH: P] gives us helpful information about the tendency of the vector field to behave like a source or a sink at [MATH: P.] We'll describe this in more detail shortly.

---

Item 3 — Example: Finding the Divergence of a Vector Field in Two Dimensions

Example Prompt:
Consider the vector field [MATH: \mathbf{F}=\ln(2x+y)\,\mathbf{i}+ x^2e^{3y}\,\mathbf{j}.]
Evaluate [MATH: \nabla \cdot\mathbf{F}] at the point [MATH: (1,0).]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
If [MATH: \mathbf{F}=P\,\mathbf{i}+Q\,\mathbf{j}] is a vector field on [MATH: \mathbb{R}^2] and the partial derivatives of the components of [MATH: \mathbf F] all exist, then the divergence of [MATH: \mathbf F] is the scalar field given by

[MATH: \nabla\cdot\mathbf{F}=\textrm{div}\,\mathbf F=\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x}+\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y}.]

Therefore, we have
[MATH: ∇ ⋅ F|= (∂P)/(∂x) + (∂Q)/(∂y); = (∂)/(∂x)(\ln (2x + y)) + (∂)/(∂y)(x^{2}e^{3y}); = (2)/(2x + y) + 3x^{2}e^{3y}.]

Finally, we evaluate [MATH: \textrm{div}\,\mathbf {F}] at the point [MATH: (1,0),] and obtain
[MATH: (∇ ⋅ F)(1, 0)|= (2)/(2(1) + 0) + 3(1)^{2}e^{3(0)}; = 1 + 3; = 4.]

---

Item 6 — Example: Finding the Divergence of a Vector Field in Three Dimensions

Example Prompt:
Consider the vector field [MATH: \mathbf{F}=(2x-y)^2\,\mathbf{i}+(3y-2z)^2\,\mathbf{j}+(x-2z)^2\,\mathbf{k}.] Evaluate [MATH: \textrm{div}\,\mathbf{F}] at the point [MATH: (1,2,1).]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
If [MATH: \mathbf{F}=P\,\mathbf{i}+Q\,\mathbf{j} + R\,\mathbf k] is a vector field on [MATH: \mathbb{R}^3] and the partial derivatives of the components of [MATH: \mathbf F] all exist, then the divergence of [MATH: \mathbf F] is the scalar field given by

[MATH: \textrm{div}\,\mathbf F = \nabla\cdot\mathbf{F}=\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x}+\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y}+\dfrac{\partial R}{\partial z}.]

Therefore, we have
[MATH: ∇ ⋅ F|= (∂P)/(∂x) + (∂Q)/(∂y) + (∂R)/(∂z); = (∂)/(∂x)((2x − y)^{2}) + (∂)/(∂y)((3y − 2z)^{2}) + (∂)/(∂z)((x − 2z)^{2}); = 4(2x − y) + 6(3y − 2z) − 4(x − 2z); = 4x + 14y − 4z.]

Finally, we evaluate [MATH: \textrm{div}\,\mathbf { F}] at the point [MATH: (1,2,1),] and obtain
[MATH: divF(1, 2, 1)|= 4(1) + 14(2) − 4(1); = 28.]

---

Item 9 — Tutorial: Physical Interpretation of Divergence

Content:
Our goal now is to develop an intuitive understanding of what the divergence of a vector field measures.

Content:
Consider the vector field [MATH: \mathbf F(x,y)] and the point [MATH: S,] shown below. Imagine that this vector field represents the velocity field of a stream of flowing water.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/0ebf9f474e4eac749e182bd3a5ca9607]

Content:
We can see from our diagram that [MATH: S] acts like a source. You can think of this as an open faucet, pushing water onto the plane and away from itself.

Content:
Since [MATH: S] acts like a source, [MATH: \textrm{div}\,\mathbf F] is nonzero. By convention, if a point [MATH: S] acts like a source, the divergence is positive:
[MATH: \textrm{div}\,\mathbf F > 0]
In this particular case, every point in our vector field acts as a source. So [MATH: \textrm{div}\,\mathbf F > 0] everywhere.

Content:
If we reverse the situation, we get the following:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/2318cee55cbaa4a0987c34237058fd13]

Content:
We can see from our diagram that [MATH: T] acts like a sink. You can think of this as an open plughole that sucks in the surrounding water.

Content:
Since [MATH: T] acts like a sink, [MATH: \textrm{div}\,\mathbf F] is also nonzero. By convention, if a point [MATH: T] acts like a sink, the divergence is negative:
[MATH: \textrm{div}\,\mathbf F < 0]
Every point in our vector field acts like a sink in this case. So [MATH: \textrm{div}\,\mathbf F < 0] everywhere.

Content:
Finally, note that if [MATH: \textrm{div}\,\mathbf F = 0] everywhere in the domain of some vector field [MATH: \mathbf F,] we say that [MATH: \mathbf F] is solenoidal.

---
